feedback: If a learner shades both whole circles for A∪B, point out the overlap has been counted twice and the running total passes 30 — the middle six can only be counted once, so the union count is A + B − A∩B.

If they shade the entire cricket circle (14) for 'cricket but NOT football', return to region naming: the overlap is 'both'; 'cricket but not football' is the cricket circle MINUS the overlap — the crescent only (8).
If they write P(cricket only) = 8/14, ask 'out of how many students altogether?' — an unconditional probability is over the whole 30, so 8/30.
If they answer 'the probability is 8' (a count), restate that a probability is a part of the whole between 0 and 1 — the region count over the total: 8 out of 30 is 8/30.
On the conditional, if they keep 30 as the denominator, ask who is being considered now — only the cricket-lovers, so the denominator is 14, not 30.
activities.intendedInsight: The overlap counts once, so the union COUNT is A + B − A∩B; and the denominator is the whole universal set unless a question conditions on a restricted subset, in which case the denominator shrinks to that subset.
learnerActions: Place 30 student tokens into a two-circle Venn (football / cricket) inside a rectangle; fill the intersection first (likes both), then the 'only' crescents (by subtracting the overlap from each set total when only totals are given), then the 'neither' region outside both circles — e.g. 12 football-only, 6 both, 8 cricket-only, 4 neither.
Check that all regions sum to 30 before reading anything off.
Name each region in words BEFORE writing notation: 'likes both' = A∩B, 'football only' = A only, 'likes either' = A∪B, 'neither' outside both.
Shade 'likes cricket but NOT football' (the cricket-only crescent, 8 students) and write its probability as 8/30 = 4/15 over the total of 30.
Shade A∪B and find its COUNT two ways: by adding region counts (12 + 6 + 8 = 26), and by checking 18 + 14 − 6 = 26 to see why the overlap is subtracted; the probability is then 26/30.
Switch to a conditional: 'among the cricket-lovers, what fraction also like football?' — identify the new denominator (14, all who like cricket) and compute 6/14.
activities.title: Build a two-circle Venn from student data, then shade and read probabilities

feedback: If a probability looks wrong, check whether every outcome was listed — a missing outcome changes both the region count and the total.

If the learner struggles to coordinate regions with individual outcomes, have them tag each listed outcome with its region before counting, so region totals are built from real outcomes rather than guessed.
activities.intendedInsight: Probabilities read off a diagram are only trustworthy when the complete set of equally likely outcomes has been enumerated and sorted correctly; the diagram organises outcomes but does not create them.
learnerActions: For a combined-events scenario, use systematic listing or the product rule to enumerate every possible outcome before sorting.
Place each enumerated outcome into the correct Venn region (or a two-way table as an alternative organiser mapping to the same four regions).

Confirm that favourable ÷ total rests on the genuine, fully-listed outcomes, and that those listed outcomes are equally likely (e.g. ordered pairs from a fair coin and a fair die, not just the possible totals of two dice). Then count the region, count the universal set and form the fraction.
Compare the Venn diagram and a two-way table of the same data to see that both encode the four regions (both, A only, B only, neither).
activities.title: Generate the full outcome set, then sort it into the diagram

feedback: If a learner adds the two circle totals for the union, ask them to point to who gets counted twice and why that inflates the total.
If they say adding 'neither' students changes no probabilities, remind them the universal-set total grew, so every probability over the whole set changes even though the circle counts did not.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbal justification surfaces the double-counting logic and the role of the denominator, reinforcing the construction skill rather than replacing it.
learnerActions: Justify each region count aloud: how many like football altogether (18, not 12), how many like cricket altogether (14), how many like both (6).

Explain in your own words why the number who like football OR cricket is 12 + 8 + 6 = 26 — and NOT 18 + 14 = 32 — because the 6 who like both are already included in each circle total; the probability is then 26/30.

State what changes and what stays the same if four more 'neither' students join: the universal-set total rises to 34, so every probability taken over the universal set changes, while the region counts for football and cricket stay fixed (and a probability taken only among cricket-lovers, like 6/14, is unaffected).
activities.title: Explain why the overlap is not counted twice (reasoning talk)
